frontMatter.title: The 60 Coupling Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points
frontMatter.description: What each of the 60 coupling mechanisms means, why it couples, how harmful it is, and why it removes the points it removes — the reference behind every score in the 65-language comparison.

frontMatterLines: title: "The 60 Coupling Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points"

description: What each of the 60 coupling mechanisms means, why it couples, how harmful it is, and why it removes the points it removes — the reference behind every score in the 65-language comparison.

blocks.q: **Companion to:** [The Great Language Smackdown](index.qmd) · [the Scoreboard and the full per-language data](scoreboard.qmd) · [the scoring model](objective-coupling-scoring-model.qmd)

blocks.p: Every language on this site is measured against **one inventory of 60 coupling mechanisms** — the same list, with the same weights, and the same arithmetic, for all 65. No language gets a private criterion, and no mechanism is applied to one language and then set aside for another. That is what makes the comparison a comparison: a difference between two scores is a difference in which mechanisms are present, never a difference in how strictly the two languages were judged.

This page explains each criterion. For every mechanism it gives what the mechanism is, what it forces to agree, how harmful it is — the weight tier that removes the points — and a concrete example. The [Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd) publishes the other half: which mechanisms each language has, and the score that follows. The [scoring model](objective-coupling-scoring-model.qmd) gives the arithmetic and the tests that decide presence.

Two parts of a program are **coupled** where they must agree about one shared thing: a type, a heap, a lock, a name space, a platform ABI, a runtime. The agreement is the cost. It has to be established when the code is written, it has to be maintained while the code lives, and it has to be re-established whenever either side changes.
A language mechanism is a **coupling criterion** when it forces agreement that the programmer cannot refuse. Three properties decide how much that costs:

rawtable: | Property | Question | Effect on the weight |
| **Breadth** | How much of the program has to agree — one call site, one module, or the whole program? | A wider agreement costs more |
| **Escape** | Can a programmer opt out of the mechanism locally? | No escape costs more |
| **Silence** | Does the language say so, or must a reader discover it? | A silent obligation costs more |

blocks.p: A mechanism that makes the whole program agree, with no local way out, and nothing in the language that records the agreement, is **High**. A mechanism that forces agreement across ordinary code, escapable only by a convention that the whole codebase must keep, is **Moderate**. A mechanism whose agreement is confined to a boundary, and removable by a contained workaround, is **Minor**.
That is the whole rationale for the weights. The tier is a judgment about **breadth, escape, and silence** — not a count of incidents, and not a substitute for measurement.

rawtable: | Tier | Weight | What the tier asserts | What saturates a dimension |
| **High** | −15 | Agreement across the whole program, no local escape, and nothing in the language that records it | One High mechanism, alone |
| **Moderate** | −8 | Agreement across ordinary code, escapable only by a whole-codebase convention | Two Moderate mechanisms |
| **Minor** | −4 | Agreement confined to a boundary, removable by a contained workaround | Four Minor mechanisms, clamped to −15 |

blocks.p: Within one dimension the present weights are added and the total is **clamped at −15**, the weight of one High mechanism. The dimension score is 100 minus that clamped total. The clamp is a rubric choice, not a measurement: it keeps the scores bounded (a dimension never costs more than one severe mechanism), monotone (adding a mechanism never improves the score), and comparable (no score collapses to zero). It is deliberate, and it is arbitrary.

Each entry gives the mechanism's code and tier, what the mechanism **is**, what it **forces to agree**, an **example**, and — where the criterion is easy to misread — what its presence does **not** mean.

Presence is a factual question about the **language**: does the language hand the programmer this construct? It is not a judgment about the code. Every language permits a global; `C1` asks whether a global is the *default* home for state.

**A check behind a project switch.** Some mechanisms depend on a compiler switch. The mark uses the configuration the language's own project initialiser writes for the version shown, because that is what a new project gets without a decision. `tsc --init` writes `"strict": true` (which sets `strictNullChecks`), so TypeScript is not charged `T10`; `dotnet new` writes `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`, so C# is not charged `T10`; Visual Basic's compiler default is `Option Strict Off` and the SDK template sets no `OptionStrict`, so the narrowing conversion is charged `T2`. Where the initialiser writes no switch, the compiler default governs. A check that only a separate tool supplies is never counted — that is what `T1` already says about `mypy` in CI.

**A mitigation is not an absence.** Some languages offer an opt-in construct that avoids a mechanism — `@CompileStatic` in Groovy, `try-with-resources` in Java, `reified` in Kotlin, a lint rule, or a flag the initialiser does not set. The mechanism stays charged, because the default code still pays it and avoiding it needs knowledge the language does not force. The model measures what the *language* imposes, not what a disciplined team can achieve. If a mitigation lowered the score, two teams on the same language would score differently, and the language would have no score. The mitigation is recorded on the language page as a strength or a trade-off, never as a discount. The line between a mitigation and an absence is the project-switch rule above.

Present weights are added within a dimension, the total is clamped at −15, and the score is 100 minus the sum of the clamped per-dimension contributions. Here is Go's Core score, from the criteria above:

Total clamped = 4 + 15 + 12 + 15 = 46. Core = 100 − 46 = **54**. The Memory and Concurrency dimensions would each have cost more than −15; the clamp holds each at the weight of one High mechanism. The [Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd) holds the same data for all 65 languages, and reproduces every score the same way.

blocks.text: What the criteria do not measure

blocks.p: The inventory prices the **language**, before any design decision, and it is honest about its limits.

ul: **Not design quality.** Two programs in the same language differ more from each other than the languages differ from one another. A program can cluster what the language scatters, and a good design decision is exactly that act. The score is the raw material, not the outcome.

**Not team skill or process.** A discipline that a team keeps — a checked build, a mandatory code review of ownership, a lint rule — can hold a High mechanism at bay in practice. The model charges it anyway, because the discipline is not in the language and cannot be relied on by the next team.

**Not severity in a particular system.** The weight judges breadth, escape, and silence. A Minor mechanism in a hot path can cost more than a High one in a corner of the program, and the model deliberately does not try to price that. A weight is a property of the mechanism; a cost is a property of a system.

**Not the last word on any one language.** Every mechanism mark is a factual claim about the language, and a factual claim can be wrong. When one is, the mark is corrected, and every score, table, and ranking derived from it is regenerated. The [Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd) carries the data so that the claim can be checked rather than trusted.

blocks.p: **The formal development.** The definitions, theorems, and proofs behind this page are published in:

ul: *On the Nature of Coupling: All Coupling as Shared Resource Access* — Zenodo, 2026 — [doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925122](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21925122)
*A Self-Contained Derivation of the Optimal Modularization from Coupling* — Zenodo, 2026 — [doi:10.5281/zenodo.21925268](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21925268)
